title: Senate Blocks Landmark Crypto Bill as Bitcoin Tumbles 4%
excerpt: The CLARITY Act's 49-50 cloture defeat on Tuesday marks the crypto industry's first major legislative loss since it spent over $300 million on the 2024 and 2026 elections.
body:
• The Senate blocked the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act in a 49-50 procedural vote on September 15, short of the 60 votes needed — with four Republicans joining all Democrats in opposition.
  • President Trump's crypto business interests and Democrats' demands for stronger ethics provisions were central sticking points, alongside opposition from the community banking lobby.
  • Bitcoin fell about 4% to roughly $75,908; Coinbase and Circle dropped 9–11% and Strategy fell 6.2%.
  • The bill is effectively dead before the November 3 midterms — Polymarket now puts the chance of it becoming law in 2026 at 14%, down from 31% before the vote.

The U.S. Senate voted down the crypto industry's top legislative priority on Tuesday, dealing the sector its first major defeat in Washington since it poured more than $300 million into the 2024 and 2026 election cycles. The motion to advance the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act — the industry's flagship market-structure bill — failed 49-50 on a procedural cloture vote, well short of the 60 votes required, with four Republicans joining all Democrats in opposition. Bloomberg Law named Sens. Susan Collins and Josh Hawley among the GOP defectors.

Why the bill failed

President Trump personally rallied crypto executives at the White House in support of the legislation — but his own entanglements helped sink it. Trump earlier this year disclosed he made well over $1 billion from crypto-linked investments, including from World Liberty Financial, the firm he co-founded, according to Barron's. Democrats demanded stronger ethics provisions barring Trump and other senior officials from profiting from crypto businesses, and revised language in a weekend draft was not enough. "The Democrats want more. They always want more. If we waited another month, they would want more. There's no end to it," said Sen. Cynthia Lummis (R-Wyo.), the bill's most visible champion, to CoinDesk.

The banking lobby supplied a second line of opposition. Community bank executives pressed Republican lawmakers to demand a stronger ban on high-yield crypto accounts that could siphon deposits away from banks, Reuters and Barron's reported — and that pressure peeled off some Republicans. A breakdown in bipartisan talks sealed the outcome: Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.), a key Democratic negotiator, accused Republicans of abruptly ending negotiations to force a vote, telling CNN "they were never serious about bipartisan negotiations."

"It takes 60 votes to pass a bill, and instead of spending their time twisting themselves into knots to appease President Trump, Republicans should have worked more closely with Senate Democrats to craft a bill that could pass with strong ethics provisions."

— Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.)

The limits of crypto's political machine

Reuters reports the industry spent more than $300 million combined on the 2024 and 2026 elections, with roughly a $130 million war chest remaining. In 2024 alone, crypto firms accounted for 48% of all corporate election spending — $119 million of $248 million — and Fairshake and its affiliates spent over $133 million, backing winners in 33 of 35 races it entered. For 2026, Fairshake reported $193 million in cash on hand after top-ups of $25 million from Ripple and $24 million from Andreessen Horowitz. But the vote showed money has limits. "The politics here changed slightly in a way that made it less difficult for the Democrats to vote against it… they don't need to fear the crypto lobby and campaign money as much as they have," Ian Katz of Capital Alpha Partners told Reuters.

Market fallout

Bitcoin fell roughly 4% on Tuesday to about $75,908, Reuters reported, and Morningstar said it touched as low as $75,026 — reversing a rally that had pushed it above $82,000 at the start of September after a roughly 25% surge between August 19 and 25. Coinbase and Circle Internet Group dropped 9–11%, Strategy fell 6.2%, and XRP and Ether slid alongside. Markets were also pricing an expected quarter-point Fed rate increase on Wednesday, a headwind for risk assets. Javier Molina of eToro warned that if bitcoin breaks below $75,000, it could slide toward $69,000–$70,000.

What comes next

The bill is effectively dead for 2026. The Senate is not expected to take it up again before the November 3 midterms, and even a successful cloture vote would have left little time to reconcile the Senate version with the House-passed bill. Reuters reports Democrats are likely to win the House, where they would focus on oversight of the Trump administration rather than crypto legislation. Prediction markets now put the chance of the Clarity Act becoming law in 2026 at just 14%, down from 31% on Monday. Industry leaders struck a defiant tone: Circle CEO Jeremy Allaire said he still believes it could become law, and Digital Chamber CEO Cody Carbone said "the fight is far from over."

For Indian crypto investors — India remains one of the world's largest retail crypto markets even as New Delhi tightened oversight with its September takedown order against offshore platforms — the U.S. regulatory rulebook that exchanges serving them operate under stays uncertain for at least another year.

nri_angle: India remains one of the world's largest retail crypto markets, so U.S. regulatory clarity — now delayed at least a year — directly affects the rulebook for exchanges serving Indian and NRI investors.
